steps.say: The face is divided into aesthetic units that share skin character. The forehead forms one unit and the eye and brow form another unit. The nose, cheek, lip, and chin form the remaining aesthetic units. Surgeons hide scar junctions along unit boundaries whenever possible. A boundary scar draws less attention than a crossing scar.
steps.tx: The face divides into **facial aesthetic units**, namely the forehead, the eye and brow region, the nose, the cheek, the lip, and the chin. Skin within one unit shares colour, texture, and thickness more closely than skin across a boundary. Surgeons hide scar junctions along unit **boundaries** whenever possible. A scar that follows a natural junction draws far less attention than a scar that crosses a unit.

rows: Forehead, eye and brow, nose, cheek, lip, chin
Hide scar junctions along unit boundaries

steps.tx: This skull shows a **fused sagittal suture** with an elongated vault, frontal bossing, and occipital bulleting, which together indicate sagittal craniosynostosis. The lower panels contrast early endoscopic **strip craniectomy** with open total **vault remodelling**. A third panel reminds the team to watch for raised intracranial pressure. Timing and technique choice remain the classic examination focus here.
steps.say: The skull shows a fused sagittal suture with an elongated vault. Frontal bossing and occipital bulleting complete the sagittal synostosis picture. Early strip craniectomy contrasts with open vault remodelling below. The team also watches for raised intracranial pressure. Timing and technique choice dominate examination questions here.

steps.say: Relaxed skin tension lines run perpendicular to mimetic muscle pull. An incision parallel to these lines is closed under less tension. Such an incision spreads less while healing progresses. A crossing incision widens and remains visible afterward. The surgeon marks the lines before cutting skin.
steps.tx: **Relaxed skin tension lines** run **perpendicular** to the pull vectors of the underlying **mimetic muscles**. Incisions placed parallel to these lines close under less tension and spread less during healing. Incisions that cross the lines widely tend to widen and remain visible. The surgeon therefore marks the lines before cutting and aligns every elective incision with them.

rows: Perpendicular to underlying mimetic muscle contracture vectors
Parallel relaxed skin tension lines to avoid spreading

steps.say: The facial nerve passes deep to the SMAS within the cheek. The layer protects the trunk during facelift dissection. Branches emerge and supply mimetic muscles from their deep surface. The wrong dissection plane causes weakness of facial expression.
steps.tx: The **facial nerve** travels **deep to the SMAS** within the cheek, where the layer protects the trunk during dissection. Branches then emerge and supply the **mimetic muscles** from their deep surface. The superficial musculoaponeurotic system therefore forms the key surgical plane in facelift surgery. Dissection in the wrong plane risks weakness of facial expression.

vis.caption: Key surgical techniques for facial aesthetic procedures

steps.say: Three mimetic muscles break the usual deep surface rule. The mentalis receives its supply on the superficial surface. The levator anguli oris and the buccinator have this exception in common. Every other mimetic muscle has its supply from the deep surface. This reversal is a favourite viva question for examiners.
steps.tx: Only three mimetic muscles receive their nerve supply on the **superficial surface**, which breaks the usual deep surface rule. They are the **mentalis**, the **levator anguli oris**, and the **buccinator**. Every other mimetic muscle receives its branch from the deep surface. This exception is a favourite viva question because it reverses the general pattern.

steps.say: The frontal branch crosses the zygomatic arch midway along the Pitanguy line. The line runs from the tragus toward the lateral canthus region. The branch runs inside temporoparietal fascia at the arch. Careless dissection causes branch injury and loss of brow elevation.
steps.tx: The **frontal branch** of the facial nerve crosses the **zygomatic arch** midway along the **Pitanguy line**, which joins the tragus to a point beyond the lateral canthus. At the arch the branch runs inside the temporoparietal fascia and remains vulnerable. Brow and forehead dissection therefore stays in a safe plane near this line. Injury silences forehead movement and brow elevation.

vis.alt: Facial nerve trunk with branches fanning over mimetic muscles, showing frontal branch territory toward the brow and forehead.
vis.caption: Facial nerve branches over mimetic muscles. Pitanguy line is in the text, not on the drawing (StewardMD).

steps.say: The marginal mandibular nerve runs superficial to the facial vessels. The nerve passes below the mandibular border near the angle. This dip exposes it during submandibular and neck dissection. Injury causes weak lower lip depression and an uneven smile.
steps.tx: The **marginal mandibular nerve** runs **superficial to the facial vessels** at the mandibular angle, where neck dissection exposes it. The nerve may dip up to **one to two centimetres below** the inferior mandibular border. This dip places it inside the field during submandibular and neck surgery. Injury weakens lower lip depression and distorts the smile.

rows: Superficial to facial vessels at the mandibular angle
Up to 1 to 2 cm below the inferior mandibular border

steps.say: The nose divides into subunits for reconstruction planning. The dorsum, tip, and columella form the central subunits. Paired sidewalls, alar lobules, and soft tissue triangles complete the map. Scars hide best along subunit seams after reconstruction. Whole subunit replacement usually looks better than patching.
steps.tx: The nose divides into **nasal subunits**, with the **dorsum, tip, and columella** placed centrally. Paired sidewalls, paired alar lobules, and paired soft tissue triangles complete the map laterally. Reconstruction respects these subunits because scars hide best along subunit seams. Replacing a whole subunit usually looks better than patching part of one subunit.

rows: Sidewalls, alar lobules, soft tissue triangles

steps.say: A defect beyond half a subunit needs whole subunit reconstruction. The surgeon excises the remaining skin of that subunit. The team reconstructs the entire subunit as one piece. A partial patch shows borders and betrays the repair. Whole unit rebuilding gives superior camouflage afterward.
steps.tx: When a nasal defect involves **more than fifty percent** of one subunit, the surgeon excises the remaining skin of that subunit. The team then reconstructs the **entire subunit** as one aesthetic piece. A partial patch shows borders inside the subunit and betrays the repair. The **fifty percent rule** therefore converts a patch problem into a cleaner whole unit rebuild.

rows: Nasal defect greater than 50% of a subunit
